attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post. The surrounding quotes of others are separate from this sentence.

semantics.note: Keeps 'seems' and the original clauses. 'Seems inevitable' signals near-certainty, not graded probability, so it is a forecast. The present-tense clauses sit inside the same 'inevitable that' frame.

contract.note: Reading collapse as a funding-driven sector collapse is fair, and the context allows further raises. No deadline or collapse measure was given, so the evaluator's reading controls.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own disclosure of $122B in committed capital (March 2026). This shows financing continued, but committed capital does not rule out an undated collapse.
xAI's own disclosure of a $6B Series C (Dec 2024). This shows investor appetite continued but does not settle an eventual collapse.

reviews.rationale: This is an undated forecast of a funding-driven collapse. The packet shows large financing continuing into 2026, which cuts against his description of lost appetite. However, the contract says continued funding cannot disprove an eventual collapse, and no documented sector collapse has happened. No deadline has passed and no conclusive event exists, so the claim stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own back-of-napkin calculation in his post.

semantics.note: This is a conditional arithmetic claim on stated assumptions (6x cost, same 35% margin). The proposition keeps both qualifiers and the per-user, per-year amount.

contract.note: Testing internal consistency against the standard definition of margin on revenue is fair and ordinary. Nothing turns on a contested interpretation.

evidence.note: A textbook definition of profit margin (profit as a share of sales). Applying it: 32.5 × 6 = 195; 195 ÷ 0.65 = 300; profit = 105; 105 ÷ 300 = 35%. The event date reflects the date of the claim, not the textbook's publication date.

reviews.rationale: With the stated inputs ($32.50 cost, 6x multiplier, 35% margin), cost comes to $195, required revenue to $300 and profit to $105, which is exactly 35% of revenue. His arithmetic holds under the independent definition. The inputs themselves are assumptions and are not being tested.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his post.

semantics.note: A present-tense observation about investor sentiment toward the AI boom and the big tech companies funding it. The normalisation drops only the word 'hype'.

contract.note: Reading the claim as visible investor concern about AI spending and payoff in July to early August 2024 is a fair, ordinary reading. It does not require unanimity.

evidence.note: Reuters, July 30, 2024: a named portfolio manager whose firm holds Microsoft shares links impatience to AI spending without matching revenue. Shares fell on the spending forecast.
Microsoft's own earnings-call transcript shows an analyst asking whether capex can slow. This reflects scrutiny but does not by itself show impatience.
Meta shares rose on a reassuring outlook. This limits how broad the impatience was but is not broad evidence of growing patience.

reviews.rationale: Contemporary Reuters reporting quotes a named investor on impatience with AI spending, and records Microsoft's share drop and Wall Street's hopes for a faster payoff. This meets the support condition. Meta's favourable reaction shows sentiment was mixed, not that patience was growing, so it does not meet the contradiction condition.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: 'I can't imagine' expresses strong disbelief, not graded probability, so this is a forecast. The 'if OpenAI does charge' antecedent is kept. The drafter's modality 'unlikely' slightly understates his firmness.

contract.note: Limiting the claim to search-specific payment, and treating a bundled subscription as charging, are reasonable choices but the speaker did not supply them. The threshold for 'aggressive' advertising is the evaluator's.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own disclosure that search became free and broadly available. It says nothing about search-specific payment of $300.
OpenAI's Go tier at $8/month (Jan 2026) meets the charging antecedent under the bundle reading. It is evidence of the condition, not of the outcome.
OpenAI's own disclosure of ad tests on the Free and Go tiers. This is a pilot only and does not show aggressive advertising on paid search.
Independent count of about 19 ads per 100 travel searches, but from a logged-out sample. It does not measure paid users or the purpose of the ads.

reviews.rationale: No deadline was given. The packet shows no search-specific purchases at $300 a year, and no clearly aggressive advertising on paid search access. Ads on the paid Go tier and the logged-out ad counts point against his expectation but do not meet the early-resolution rule. The forecast is open and unsettled.
